track.name: people
track.label: People & Org Design
track.summary: Go from first-time manager to org design and people analytics — the hiring, feedback, performance, and structure skills every people leader actually uses.

phases.title: Foundations of People Management
phases.description: The mental and behavioral shift from doing the work yourself to getting it done through other people.

phases.title: Hiring & Talent Acquisition
phases.description: Attracting the right candidates and running an interview process that actually predicts who will succeed.

phases.title: Performance Management & Feedback
phases.description: Setting clear goals, giving honest feedback, and handling performance problems before they get bigger.

phases.title: Organizational Design & Team Structure
phases.description: How reporting lines, team boundaries, and career ladders shape what actually gets done.

phases.title: Culture, DEI & Employee Experience
phases.description: The practices that make people want to stay, contribute, and do their best work.

phases.title: People Analytics & HR Operations
phases.description: The data, pay structures, and operational plumbing that keep a people function running.

topics.title: From Individual Contributor to Manager
topics.description: Why the job changes completely once your results come through other people's work instead of your own.

steps.d: Reflect on your transition to manager: what surprised you, what took more time than you expected, and what you wish you'd known.
Find a task you're still doing that your report could own; describe what's preventing you from handing it off (trust, time, clarity).
Schedule a 30-minute 1:1 with one report focused on their priorities, challenges, and what they need from you to succeed.
Define one clear goal for your team for the next quarter (outcome, owner, deadline) and explain why it matters to the business.
Identify a performance or behavior issue with one report, schedule a conversation, and deliver specific feedback on what to change.

topics.title: 1:1s & Ongoing Feedback
topics.description: Running a recurring 1:1 that's actually useful, and giving feedback your report can act on.

steps.d: Design a 30-minute 1:1 template covering: their wins/challenges last week, your feedback or coaching, their growth/career thoughts, action items.
Before your next 1:1, review your report's work from the last week and write three specific things you want to discuss or praise.
Tell a report one specific thing they did well this week, describe the impact, and explain why it matters (not just 'good job').
When your report makes a mistake, describe what happened, the impact, what they should have done, and what you need to see differently.
When you and your report disagree, explain your perspective, ask theirs, find common ground, and show how you weighed their input in your decision.

topics.title: Delegation & Trust
topics.description: Handing off real ownership of work instead of just tasks, and building the trust that makes it stick.

steps.d: Assign a real project or outcome to one report and be explicit: the end goal, their decision-making authority, where they should escalate, and your role.
When a report struggles with an assignment, resist fixing it yourself; ask questions to help them find the solution.
Set up one check-in point during a project (25% done) to verify progress without reviewing every decision they make.
When a report completes a project or ownership task, acknowledge their effort, the impact, and how this shows their growth.
Identify something your report is anxious about and gradually increase their ownership and authority until they feel capable.

topics.title: Writing Job Descriptions & Sourcing
topics.description: Writing a job ad that attracts the right candidates, then finding the ones who aren't applying.

steps.d: Draft a job description for a role you're hiring, including: core responsibilities (3-5), key skills, experience level, and reporting line.
For your role, clearly separate non-negotiable requirements from preferences; prioritize the top three must-haves.
Identify three channels (job boards, referral networks, communities, university lists) where candidates who match your profile actually spend time.
Write one or two short-answer questions for your application form that filter for the skill or trait that's hardest to train.
After 20-30 applications, assess your sourcing: Are you getting qualified candidates? If not, which channel underperformed?

topics.title: Structured Interviewing
topics.description: Asking every candidate the same well-designed questions and scoring them against a shared rubric.

steps.d: For each key skill or trait you need (technical depth, communication, collaboration, problem-solving), write one behavioral question and scoring criteria (1-5).
Interview three candidates for the same role using identical questions, in the same order, so you can fairly compare their responses.
Right after each interview, score the candidate on your rubric (1-5 per dimension) while details are fresh, don't wait.
After interviewing multiple candidates, lay out scorecards side by side and identify clear gaps (one excels at X, another at Y).
When you pick a candidate, be able to explain which dimensions they scored highest on and why that mattered for this role.

topics.title: Reducing Bias in Hiring
topics.description: Where bias actually creeps into a hiring process, and the concrete changes that reduce it.

steps.d: Review your last 10 job postings and applicant lists: Are you using coded language (energetic, culture fit, native English)? Are applicants diverse?
Take one hiring channel you use and adjust it: if you only referral-hire, you'll hire people like current employees; broaden your sourcing.
Replace subjective questions (Tell me about yourself) with behavioral ones (Describe a time you led change) scored against a rubric.
Have one person review applications with names and schools redacted, scoring only on experience and skills; compare to typical screening.
After each hiring round, count: What % of your interviews went to women, underrepresented groups, and non-traditional backgrounds?

topics.title: Setting Goals (OKRs)
topics.description: Pairing a clear objective with a small set of measurable key results so everyone knows what matters.

steps.d: For one report or team, define 2-3 business outcomes for the quarter (what will be different? By how much? By when?).
For each objective, write 2-3 key results that would prove success (e.g., 'increase on-time delivery from 92% to 96%' not 'improve delivery').
Explain to your report why their OKRs matter to the company and how their work connects to bigger goals.
Every Monday, review the previous week's progress on each key result and discuss blockers or adjustments needed.
At the end of the quarter, score each key result (did you hit it?) and discuss what worked, what didn't, and next quarter's goals.

topics.title: Performance Reviews
topics.description: Turning a stretch of observations into a review that's specific, fair, and doesn't surprise anyone.

steps.d: Keep a simple document and add feedback throughout the year: projects completed, problems solved, collaboration wins, areas to grow.
For a report, ask 3-5 people who work with them (peer, direct report, customer, cross-function) one open question: what should they keep doing, start doing, stop doing.
For a report not meeting expectations, write whether the issue is skill (they don't know how), will (they're not trying), or environment (they lack tools/support).
Draft a performance review that's honest about both strengths and gaps, with specific examples for each, and a development focus for the next period.
In the review meeting, don't surprise them; your feedback should match what you've shared in 1:1s throughout the period.

topics.title: Managing Underperformance
topics.description: Naming a performance problem directly and working through a structured plan to fix it.

steps.d: When someone is underperforming, write specifically what's not meeting the standard: quality, speed, reliability, collaboration, or something else.
Before you assume they can't do the job, diagnose whether the issue is personal capability, unclear expectations, missing tools, or a personal crisis.
Document a 30- or 60-day plan: the specific behavior/outcome that needs to change, how you'll support them (training, coaching, resources), and how you'll measure progress.
Meet with them every week during the plan to discuss progress, barriers, wins, and any adjustments to their support or the plan.
At the end of the plan, decide: are they improving sufficiently to stay, or is it time for a transition conversation?

topics.title: Organizational Design Fundamentals
topics.description: The models and tradeoffs behind how a company groups people into teams and reporting lines.

steps.d: Draw your org: boxes for roles/departments, lines showing reporting relationships, and labels for team sizes and functions.
Is your org built by function (engineering, sales, ops), by customer (SMB, enterprise, partners), by geography, or by product? Name it.
Does your current structure help or hinder your strategy? For example, if you want to move fast, are you too functional? Too siloed?
Identify one communication gap, duplicate effort, or slow decision in your org and trace it back to structure (wrong reporting line, too many layers).
Propose one structural change (merge teams, create a new role, adjust reporting lines) and explain how it would fix the weakness.

topics.title: Span of Control & Team Topologies
topics.description: How many people one manager can actually manage well, and how team shape affects how work flows.

steps.d: For each manager in your org, count their direct reports; if it's >7-10, they're probably overloaded or under-coaching.
Find one person who has to approve too many decisions or know too much; describe what they're a bottleneck for.
Describe your team structure (co-located, distributed, cross-functional, dedicated) and how it affects communication and decision-making speed.
If your team structure is causing silos, propose one change (different reporting line, shared goals, co-located sprint, weekly sync) to improve flow.
Implement a small structural change (create a new role, merge two teams, add a sync meeting) and measure its impact after 4 weeks.

topics.title: Career Ladders & Leveling
topics.description: Defining what each level of seniority actually means so growth and pay decisions aren't arbitrary.

steps.d: For your organization, write what each level (IC1/2/3/4, manager/senior/director/VP) actually means in terms of scope, impact, and skills.
Build a simple grid showing what's expected of each level for: scope of decisions, people managed, strategic impact, technical depth, and collaboration.
Take a current employee and honestly assess which level they're at based on your matrix; compare to their title and compensation.
When someone is ready to advance, show them the next level's matrix, get agreement on what they need to demonstrate, and give them time to grow into it.
Review your current compensation and titles: are similar levels paid similarly, or are there unexplained gaps? If gaps, document why or fix them.

topics.title: Building Team Culture
topics.description: Turning stated values into the everyday norms a team actually follows.

steps.d: What does your team or company say it values (excellence, trust, speed, creativity, customer focus)? Write down 3-5 stated values.
For one stated value, observe what behaviors actually get rewarded, celebrated, and practiced; compare to what you claim to value.
If your stated values don't match observed behavior, describe one norm or practice that's killing that value (e.g., claiming speed but celebrating caution).
Pick one value you want to strengthen and change your own behavior visibly to model it; describe what you'll do and stop doing.
To build culture, change one system (hiring rubric, recognition process, project selection, meeting norms) to reward the behavior you want.

topics.title: Diversity, Equity & Inclusion Fundamentals
topics.description: The core DEI vocabulary and concepts — diversity, equity, inclusion, bias, and belonging — and why they're distinct.

steps.d: In your own words, explain: diversity (who's in the room), equity (fair treatment and outcomes), inclusion (belongs and heard), and belonging (safe and valued).
Name where bias can creep in: hiring, promotion, project assignment, 1:1 time, compensation, speaking-up norms, meeting dynamics.
Pick your hiring or promotion process and trace it for bias: Do certain groups advance at different rates? Are there coded words in job descriptions?
Talk to someone in your organization who has a different background or identity; ask what's worked well and what's been harder for them.
Based on what you've learned, propose one change (expanded sourcing, adjusted rubric, mentor program, working group) to improve equity or inclusion.

topics.title: Employee Engagement & Retention
topics.description: What actually drives people to stay and do good work, and how to measure it honestly.

steps.d: Run or analyze an engagement survey (not just ask your direct report); measure pride in work, alignment with mission, and intent to stay.
Who on your team is most likely to leave in the next year? What would make them stay? Ask them directly if appropriate.
Analyze your engagement data: is the issue compensation, career growth, manager, work environment, or misalignment with values?
When someone leaves, conduct an exit interview and ask honestly: What could we have done differently? Would you come back?
Based on engagement data and exit interviews, implement one change likely to improve retention (flexible work, clearer growth path, better manager coaching).

topics.title: People Analytics Fundamentals
topics.description: Using workforce data to test assumptions about hiring, performance, and retention instead of guessing.

steps.d: Identify key metrics for your team or company: headcount, turnover rate, time-to-hire, internal promotion rate, compensation equity, engagement score.
For one metric (turnover, time-to-hire), research typical benchmarks and compare your organization; if you're an outlier, ask why.
Is your high turnover correlated with low engagement scores? Does faster promotion go with higher retention? Plot one relationship and interpret it.
If you believe something drives retention (remote work, manager quality, growth opportunity), pull your data and see if it actually correlates.
Use people analytics to argue for a new program (benefits change, manager training, career ladder redesign) showing the problem and potential impact.

topics.title: Compensation & Leveling Basics
topics.description: How salary bands and a compensation philosophy keep pay consistent, fair, and defensible.

steps.d: For roles you hire regularly, research salaries using Levels.fyi, Payscale, Glassdoor, or your industry survey; document by role and location.
For three roles (junior, mid, senior), define a salary range covering local market median, your company size, and profitability.
Document your approach: percentile (50th, 75th), role-based or individual, equity/bonus formula, and how you handle geographic differences.
Pull compensation data and check: Are similar levels paid similarly? Is there an unexplained gender/race pay gap? Do you have justifiable outliers?
If you find unfair pay, decide: Do you adjust this year or phase it in? How do you fund it? What's your communication plan?

topics.title: HR Operations & Compliance Basics
topics.description: The recurring administrative and legal-compliance work that keeps a people function out of trouble.

steps.d: List every recurring HR task: onboarding, benefits, payroll, tax, compliance updates, reviews, and approvals; identify the owner and timing.
For your headcount and jurisdiction, list the three statutes that apply most (employment law, tax, benefits, safety, anti-discrimination) and name who signs off.
For one compliance area (hiring, pay, benefits, separation), ask: Are we doing this correctly? What could go wrong if we didn't?
Pick one process (hiring, offboarding, benefits enrollment) and verify it complies with law and your policies; fix any gaps.
Gather documentation showing your compliance: contracts, offer letters, termination paperwork, payroll records, benefits compliance, and policy acknowledgments.
